A breaking yoke changes who must fear

The book of Jonah showed Nineveh spared. Nahum speaks in a later time about its fall. Verse 3 still calls the LORD slow to anger. It adds that he will not clear the guilty. Verses 7 and 8 set a refuge beside a flood. Verse 13 is spoken to Judah, which lived under Assyria’s demands (2 Kings 18:14). A broken yoke changes who has reason to fear.
The predator's den becomes a place of flight

Verses 11–12 picture Nineveh as a den of lions. The lion killed enough for his cubs and his mates. He filled his caves with prey. So the city’s great wealth was plunder taken from others. Verse 9 shows that same treasure being carried off in turn. The question about the den is a taunt. Verse 13 says the voices of Assyria’s envoys will be heard no more.
The ending explains why no one offers comfort

Verse 7 asks who will mourn Nineveh or comfort her. Verse 19 gives the answer and the reason. Everyone who hears of her fall applauds. The verse ends with a question: who has not felt her endless cruelty? The applause is the verdict of her victims. Verses 8–10 recall the fall of Thebes as a warning. The book of Jonah also ends with a question about this city.
